To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
binary mergers of present day Milky-Way-like galaxies do not form giant ellipticals and that binary mergers could form intermediate-mass ellipticals if they occurred earlier than ≈ 4 Gyr ago.

the progenitors of disk galaxies do not have enough mass in metals to form giant ellipticals and that the mass of metals in disk galaxies grows too slowly with time to form the most massive early-type galaxies.

the stellar populations of Milky Way–like disks are too metal poor, too young, and too blue to be the progenitors of giant ellipticals, and that the stellar mass in metals of disk galaxies is too low to account for the observed stellar mass in metals in elliptical galaxies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the stellar populations of the progenitors (disk galaxies) and descendants (giant ellipticals) of binary mergers.
the question of whether disk galaxies could be the progenitors of giant ellipticals.
understanding the formation of the stellar populations in elliptical galaxies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
binary disk galaxy mergers are not the dominant formation mechanism of giant elliptical galaxies.
the progenitors of giant early-type galaxies were not present-day disk galaxies, but rather were more massive and metal-rich disk galaxies.
the progenitors of disk galaxies cannot have formed present-day giant elliptical galaxies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the stellar populations of present-day disk and early-type galaxies are too different to allow a scenario in which the progenitors of disk galaxies are the main contributors to the stellar mass of giant elliptical galaxies.
disk galaxies are unlikely to be the progenitors of giant elliptical galaxies.
binary disk mergers can form present-day ellipticals if they occurred at redshifts z > 2–3.
The main takeaway from our work is that

binary mergers of presentday disk galaxies cannot form present-day giant ellipticals, and the stellar populations of present-day disk and giant elliptical galaxies cannot have evolved in a similar fashion.
the progenitors of disk galaxies are not likely to be the progenitors of giant ellipticals.
the progenitors of the present-day disk galaxies are not the progenitors of giant elliptical galaxies.
